newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro bourses mixed, anxious over U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro bourses mixed, anxious over U.S. data.

text.p: European stocks started mixed on Friday with investors anxious over whether U.S. employment figures later in the day would show subdued inflation pressures.
On currency markets, the dollar began the European session stronger against the mark but slightly down on the yen after remarks by a senior German central banker supporting the Japanese currency.
Most European bourses made a strong start apart from London, which slipped slightly on interest rate jitters as data on Britain's economic performance in October registered an 18-month high.

German and Swiss stocks advanced after Wall Street posted solid gains overnight on the strength of Thursday's U.S. data suggesting a slowing in the economy, good news for interest rates. Paris was closed because of the All Saints holiday.
London investors took fright when Britain's Purchasing Managers' Index -- a key guide to economic performance -- rose to 54.5 percent in October from 53.5 percent in September.
As London's FTSE index dipped on these figures, investors joined the rest of Europe switching attention to the U.S. data due at 1330 GMT for clues on the health of the world's biggest economy.
"Most people are betting on a benign number out of the U.S.," said one dealer. "If we get it, I think we'll see most markets rally. I don't think we've seen the (stock market's) peaks yet."

The U.S. employment data is watched closely because of its global influence. When June's healthy U.S. payroll data stoked fears of higher interest rates, Wall Street suffered its seventh biggest drop ever, with consequent chaos on European bourses.
In Frankfurt, most investors took an optimistic view. Early floor trading was up nearly one percent, encouraged by Wall Street's strong perfromance and stronger bonds market.
But volumes were thin because of a holiday in most areas of Germany and some investors were reluctant to stick their necks out ahead of the U.S. figures.
The dollar climbed half a pfennig against the mark but was slightly weaker against the yen because of a knock-on effect as the Japanese currency strengthened against the mark.
The mark fell against the yen after Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said a strong yen against the mark would help German exporters.

"The latest pattern is simply to trade off the latest comment you see on the screen -- and the last comment was Welteke's," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "Basically he was talking the deutschemark down."
Currency traders were also awaiting the non-farm payrolls figures, the final instalment of the week's heavy schedule of U.S. data.
Although U.S. equity markets have in the past reacted wildly to payrolls data that was out of line with expectations, currency markets have tended to be calmer.
"I think the dollar will react to any kind of interest rate sentiment, barring some big asset price move," said David Bloom, U.S. economist at HSBC James Capel in London.
CURRENCIES AT 1030 GMT
The dollar was trading around 1.5195 marks and 113.60 yen versus 1.5132 and 113.77 in late European business on Thursday.
STOCKS AT 1030 GMT
London's FTSE 100 index was down 7.4 points at 3,971.7.
Germany's DAX index was up 22.55 lower at 2,681.80.
In Paris, markets were closed because of the holiday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $377.35 an ounce, compared to Thursday's close of $379.75. Silver was weaker at $4.80, down six cents.
